paras: The attempted lynching of Berry Henry took place in Bartow, Polk County, Florida, on the night of December 24, 1903, when 25 to 35 armed men marched to the jail and demanded Henry, a Black prisoner suspected of shooting Colonel John Beatty and his wife that morning. Sheriff J. D. Tillis refused to give up the prisoner and threatened to fire, and the men dispersed; Henry was then moved to Tampa. Headlines praised the sheriff for saving his prisoner from a mob.

Beatty, spelled "Beaty" in several reports, was general manager of the Green Bay Phosphate Company. According to an Associated Press dispatch from Bartow dated December 24, he was driving to his mines that morning when he was shot from ambush by a Black man he had discharged the day before, and Mrs. Beatty, riding with him, was struck in the face and breast. Posses searched the woods all day, and late that afternoon a Black man "supposed to be the right man" was captured and jailed at Bartow, to be taken to Beatty for identification.

Shortly after dark that Thursday, according to a Bartow dispatch of December 26, about 25 or 30 men "armed to the teeth" marched into the town to get Henry. With guns pointed at the sheriff, they told him to get out of the way and let them have the prisoner; he answered that if they came closer they would do so at their peril. The men dispersed after being assured that Henry would be taken before Beatty for identification as soon as possible.

Fearing another attempt to lynch him, the sheriff had Henry moved the next night, when officers drove him to Pridgen and boarded a train for Tampa. A Tampa dispatch of December 28 instead said that Polk County deputy sheriff Bert Childs took Henry from the jail because of mob attempts to break in, and that a mob pursued them twenty miles through the woods on Sunday, "bent on lynching the negro," before they reached Tampa that night.

Mrs. Beatty's skull was fractured, and the December 26 dispatch said it was not certain she would recover; the Ocala Banner later called her "probably fatally hurt." The Savannah Morning News set out the officers' case against Henry: a ten-bore gun and matching shot, wadding that City Marshal Childs said he found at the scene and matched to Henry's shells, and a footprint of Henry's size leading toward his home. No report of an identification, indictment or trial of Henry, or of any action against the armed men, appears in the coverage.

The episode was reported chiefly through the Associated Press dispatch from Bartow dated December 26, which ran on December 27 in the Raleigh News & Observer, the Savannah Morning News, the Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Worcester Spy, and on December 28 in the Atlanta Constitution. Headlines centered on the sheriff: the News & Observer ran "Sheriff of Nerve: He Defies and Threatens Mob and Saves His Prisoner," and the Savannah paper "The Coolness of Tillis, However, Thwarted the Mob at Bartow." The fuller versions credited the sheriff's "dogged determination" with preventing a raid on the jail, and the Savannah Morning News added, without attribution, that there was "pretty strong circumstantial evidence against the negro."

None of the reports named the armed men or gave their race, while Henry appeared throughout as "the negro." Details shifted between papers: the Birmingham Age-Herald reversed the prisoner's name to "Henry Berry," and the Worcester Spy datelined the story "Barlow." The Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier in Iowa printed the Tampa dispatch under "Florida Sheriff Foils Mob," the Berea Citizen in Kentucky and the Ocala Banner noted only the shooting, and no Black-press coverage was found.

The Bartow dispatch put Henry's removal to Tampa on the night of December 25 by train, while the Tampa dispatch put his arrival on the night of December 27 after a chase through the woods. The size of the band varies from about 25 in the Atlanta Constitution to 35 in the Montgomery Advertiser, and Childs appears as city marshal in the Savannah Morning News but as a deputy sheriff in the Tampa dispatch.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Berry Henry
bases: An armed band of 25-35 men marched to the Bartow jail and demanded the Black prisoner Berry Henry in order to lynch him, and a later dispatch says a mob chased him and his guard through the woods; no one was killed (A2, A3, A4, A9).

The papers describe an attempted lynching: an armed group of 25 or more men, with no lawful authority, sought to seize Henry over the shooting of the Beattys, but the sheriff turned them away and Henry was taken to Tampa alive (A2, A3, A9). No one was killed, so the standard definition is not met.

The Bartow AP dispatch of Dec. 26, carried in several versions (A2, A3, A4, A8), and a separate Tampa dispatch of Dec. 28 (A9) both report a mob trying to get Henry from the Bartow jail, though they differ on how he reached Tampa.

accounts.label: Bartow AP dispatch, Dec. 26
accounts.gist: Armed men marched on the jail the night of the shooting, the sheriff faced them down, they dispersed on a promise of identification, and Henry was driven to Pridgen and by train to Tampa the next night.

accounts.label: Tampa dispatch, Dec. 28
accounts.gist: Deputy Bert Childs took Henry from the jail because of mob attempts to break in, and a mob chased them twenty miles through the woods on Sunday before they reached Tampa.

accounts.label: Officers' case against Henry
accounts.gist: His ten-bore gun, matching shot, wadding found by City Marshal Childs, and a footprint leading toward his home were offered as circumstantial evidence.

framing.detail: Wire versions headlined the sheriff's defense of the prisoner ('Sheriff of Nerve', 'Sheriff Protects Prisoner', 'Attempt To Lynch Negro') without describing the armed men beyond their number.
The Savannah Morning News praised 'The Coolness of Tillis' while presenting the officers' evidence as 'pretty strong circumstantial evidence against the negro'.

conflicts.note: All versions of one Bartow dispatch; the number is not settled.
